justification_text:
The point estimates at each forecast horizon—one day, one week, and one month—are driven by the underlying trends and patterns within the data, along with gradual adjustments for how we expect uncertainty to unfold over time. For the near-term, such as the one-day forecast, the point estimate of 61.1 is heavily influenced by recent observations. At that short horizon, there’s limited opportunity for large deviations, so the forecast essentially reflects recent momentum and any detectable short-term trends. As the horizon extends to one week, I’ve incorporated more room for moderate variability or shifts based on medium-term factors, which is why the point estimate shows a slight increase to 61.5, suggesting a trend in that direction. By one month, the forecast adjusts further to 62.0, incorporating both the previously observed trend and an expectation of how certain structural patterns might play out over a longer period.

The widths of the confidence intervals reflect the uncertainty associated with each time horizon. For the one-day forecast, the interval is relatively narrow (60.0 to 62.2) because short-term predictions face fewer unknowns and are based heavily on recent, reliable data. At one week, the uncertainty grows (59.8 to 63.2) because more variables—such as external influences or noise—have had time to come into play, making the forecast inherently less precise. Over the one-month period, the confidence interval widens significantly (58.0 to 66.0), reflecting the many compounding unknowns that accumulate in the longer term. These include potential shifts in underlying drivers, surprises, or deviations from historical patterns that are harder to predict the farther out we look.

As for risks or events that could push outcomes outside of these stated intervals, those would typically be low-probability, high-impact occurrences—essentially, unexpected developments that break from historical trends or norms I’ve incorporated into the model. For example, major geopolitical events, sudden economic shocks, or extraordinary market volatility could all drive the outcomes well beyond the forecast ranges. Similarly, if the system being analyzed is subject to intrinsic volatility or structural disruption, these might exceed what the model accounts for. While the confidence intervals aim to capture the most likely range of outcomes, unforeseen events will always pose a possibility of forecasts being off-mark.
